Chapter 11 · 第十一章

Beyond Tech Lead: Charting Your Career Path技术负责人之后：规划你的职业路径

— PDF p.355 —

If you've been in the tech lead role for a while and you're ready to grow into your next stage, or even if you're just curious about what's possible, this chapter will help you explore your options.

如果你已经担任技术负责人一段时间，准备好迈入下一个阶段；又或者你只是好奇未来还有哪些可能，本章会帮你把这些选项一一梳理清楚。

There's no single direction you're supposed to go from here.

从这里出发，并没有一条“你本该走”的唯一方向。

Some people choose to stay in the tech lead role a bit longer, perhaps taking on a new challenge: leading a different team, working in a new domain, scaling up to a larger group, or trying it at another company.

有些人选择在技术负责人的岗位上再待一段时间，或许是迎接一项新的挑战：带领一支不同的团队、进入一个新的业务领域、把职责扩大到更大的团队，或是换一家公司再做一次。

Others transition fully into people management, dive deeper into technical leadership, or explore entirely different ways of leading, through programs, strategy, or consulting.

另一些人则彻底转向人员管理，或深耕技术领导力，又或者去探索全然不同的领导方式——比如通过项目群管理、战略工作或咨询顾问。

Before you make any big decisions, this chapter invites you to reflect on your experience so far, get honest about what you've loved (and what you haven't), and evaluate your strengths and areas for growth. From there, I'll explore the most common career paths after tech lead and how to approach the transition in a thoughtful, low-pressure way.

在你做出任何重大决定之前，本章邀请你先回顾迄今为止的经历，诚实地面对自己喜欢什么（以及不喜欢什么），并评估自己的优势与待成长之处。在此基础上，我会探讨技术负责人之后最常见的几条职业路径，以及如何以一种从容、低压力的方式去面对这次转型。

Your next step doesn't need to be permanent. It doesn't even need to be perfect. It just needs to move you closer to the kind of work, and the kind of impact, that feels right for you.

你的下一步不必是终身定论，甚至不必完美。它只需要让你离那种“对你来说刚刚好”的工作方式和影响力，更近一点。

Let's dive right in.

那我们这就开始吧。

Reflecting on Your Experience as a Tech Lead回顾你作为技术负责人的经历

Before you can figure out where to go next, it's worth pausing to take stock of where you've been.

在弄清楚下一步该往哪走之前，值得先停下来盘点一下自己一路走来的轨迹。

— PDF p.356 —

The tech lead role is rich with learning, about systems, about people, and, often, about yourself. Maybe you stepped into it with curiosity. Maybe it was handed to you without much preparation. However you got here, now's your chance to look back and ask, What has this role taught me? What have I enjoyed most? What has felt draining?

技术负责人这个岗位能带给你丰厚的学习——关于系统、关于人，往往也关于你自己。也许你是带着好奇走进来的；也许它是在你毫无准备的情况下被交到手上的。无论你是如何走到今天的，现在正是回头追问的时机：这个角色教会了我什么？我最享受的是什么？又是什么让我感到心力交瘁？

This section is not about evaluation in the performance review sense but about self-awareness. The kind that helps you understand what kind of work brings out your best, what kind of impact you want to have, and what kind of roles might be a better fit going forward.

本节不是要做绩效评估意义上的“考核”，而是关于自我觉察——那种能帮你看清：什么样的工作最能激发你的潜能、你想要产生怎样的影响、以及往后什么样的岗位可能更适合你的觉察。

You don't need perfect answers, just honest ones.

你不需要完美的答案，只需要诚实的答案。

Understand What You Enjoy (and Don't) About the Role弄清楚你喜欢（和不喜欢）这个角色的哪些方面

Before you decide what's next in your career, it's important to pause and reflect: what has this role actually felt like for you?

在决定职业生涯的下一步之前，重要的是停下来想一想：这个角色对你而言，实际体验究竟是什么样的？

Stepping into technical leadership is a big shift. You probably entered the role with some expectations, maybe even excitement, about the opportunity to lead, guide, and create impact beyond just the code.

迈入技术领导力是一次巨大的转变。你当初接手这个岗位时，心里大概带着一些期待，甚至是兴奋——期待有机会去领导、去引导、去创造代码之外的影响力。

But expectations and reality often don't align. This section is your chance to make sense of that gap. What surprised you? What challenged you? What inspired you?

但期待与现实往往并不吻合。本节就是让你好好消化这道落差的机会。有什么让你意外？有什么让你感到挑战？又有什么曾激励过你？

To begin this reflection, it helps to break it down into a few key areas:

要开启这场反思，可以把它拆成几个关键方面来逐一梳理：

What you've enjoyed most你最享受的是什么

Start by thinking about what you've genuinely enjoyed. Which parts of the role gave you energy? Maybe it was delegating a task to a team member and watching them grow. Maybe it was working across functions to align on a complex project. Maybe it was having more visibility into business decisions and helping translate them into technical action.

先从回想你真正享受过的事情开始。这个岗位的哪些部分曾给你注入能量？也许是把一项任务授权给团队成员、看着他成长起来；也许是跨职能协作、就一个复杂项目达成共识；又或者是能更近距离地看到业务决策，并帮着把它们转化成技术上的行动。

Try to remember the full picture, not just the highlights. It's easy to forget the frustrating parts, like long meetings, messy handovers, endless alignment. Sometimes it's not the task we miss but the outcome. You might think you miss coding, but what you're really chasing is the dopamine hit of completing a task and shipping something real to users. That kind of quick feedback loop is much harder to come by in leadership work, where progress is slower and impact unfolds over time.

试着回忆完整的画面，而不只是那些高光时刻。那些令人挫败的部分——冗长的会议、乱糟糟的交接、没完没了的对齐——很容易被我们忘掉。有时候，我们怀念的并不是任务本身，而是任务带来的结果。你也许以为自己怀念写代码，但你真正追逐的，其实是“完成一项任务、把真实的东西交付到用户手上”时那种多巴胺式的快感。而在领导力工作中，这种快速反馈循环要难得多：进展更缓慢，影响力要随时间慢慢展开。

Focus on the difference between the work you enjoy and the results that motivate you. Most meaningful work comes with some grind; the key is knowing which trade-offs you're OK with.

要分清“你享受的工作本身”和“激励你的结果”之间的差别。大多数有意义的工作都伴随着一定的苦差事；关键在于，你要清楚自己愿意接受哪些取舍。

— PDF p.357 —

Ask yourself: "What outcomes feel most rewarding?," "What parts of the process am I willing to tolerate?," and "What stays energizing, even when it's hard?" If you had a day full of just one kind of task, which type would leave you feeling accomplished and motivated? Pay attention to those moments; they're pointing you toward the kind of work you may want more of in the future.

问问自己：“什么样的结果最让我有成就感？”“流程中的哪些部分是我愿意忍受的？”以及“即使很辛苦，什么仍然让我保持干劲？”如果有一整天都只做某一种任务，哪一种会让你觉得充实又有动力？留意这些瞬间，它们正在为你指向那种“未来你可能想多做一些”的工作。

What felt most draining最让你心力交瘁的是什么

Just as important is identifying what drained you. What parts of the role made you feel stuck, frustrated, or depleted?

同样重要的，是找出那些耗尽你精力的东西。这个岗位的哪些部分让你感到卡住、沮丧，或是精疲力竭？

For some tech leads, it's endless context switching. For others, it's people challenges that never seem to resolve. Maybe you found stakeholder alignment exhausting or struggled with the lack of deep technical focus. The point is to notice patterns.

对有些技术负责人来说，那是没完没了的上下文切换；对另一些人来说，则是那些似乎永远解决不完的人的问题。也许你觉得和干系人对齐耗人心力，又或者苦于无法深入专注于技术。重点在于去发现其中的规律。

Ask yourself: was it draining because I lacked the skills, or because the task itself didn't suit me? That distinction matters because if it's a skill gap, you can grow. But if it's a values mismatch or a persistent energy drain, it might signal the kind of work you don't want to prioritize going forward.

问问自己：它之所以耗人，是因为我缺少相应的技能，还是因为这项任务本身就不适合我？这个区分很关键——如果是技能缺口，你可以去成长补足；但如果是价值观上的错配，或是一种持续性的能量消耗，那它可能在提示你：往后这类工作，你不想再把它放在优先位置。

How the role has changed you这个角色如何改变了你

Being a tech lead changes how you think. It forces you to zoom out, make trade-offs, and weigh people and delivery with equal weight. You likely developed new muscles: influence without authority, coaching under pressure, managing complexity across people and systems.

担任技术负责人会改变你的思考方式。它迫使你拉远视角、做出取舍，并把“人”和“交付”放在同等重要的天平上衡量。你很可能练出了一些新的能力：在没有职权的情况下施加影响、在压力之下进行辅导、在人与系统之间管理复杂局面。

How has your view of leadership evolved? How do you show up differently now than when you first started? What would your past self find surprising about how you operate today?

你对领导力的看法发生了怎样的演变？和刚接手时相比，你现在的行事方式有哪些不同？你过去的自己，会对你今天的做法感到哪些意外？

Signs of growth成长的迹象

It's easy to overlook your own growth, especially in a fast-paced environment. Take a moment to recognize how far you've come.

我们很容易忽视自己的成长，尤其是在快节奏的环境里。花一点时间，认可一下自己已经走了多远。

What felt hard or intimidating at first that now feels manageable or even easy? Maybe it was having tough conversations. Maybe it was leading architecture reviews. Maybe it was just knowing how to spend your time each day without a task list.

有什么事情起初让你觉得困难或望而生畏，如今却变得从容、甚至轻松？也许是进行那些艰难的谈话；也许是主持架构评审；又或者仅仅是——在没有任务清单的情况下，也知道该如何安排每一天的时间。

What feedback have you received, even informally, that points to your growth? Sometimes a team member saying "Thanks, I felt really supported" is more telling than a formal review.

你收到过哪些反馈——哪怕是非正式的——能说明你的成长？有时候，一位团队成员一句“谢谢，我觉得很有支撑感”，比一份正式评审更能说明问题。

— PDF p.358 —

Try this: write down three specific examples of things that used to feel difficult but no longer do. Include what changed, such as skills you built, confidence you gained, or support systems you leaned on. These stories are powerful evidence of growth, and they'll be helpful when building your development plan or preparing for performance reviews.

不妨试试这样做：写下三个具体的例子，记录那些曾经让你觉得困难、如今已不再为难的事情。写清楚是什么改变了——比如你练就的某项技能、获得的某份信心，或是你所依靠的支持系统。这些故事是成长的有力证据，在你制定发展计划或准备绩效评审时，都会派上用场。

What you're curious about next接下来你对什么感到好奇

Finally, let your curiosity guide you. What do you want more of? Less of? Are there parts of this role that sparked interest in something else—product, engineering management, staff engineering?

最后，让好奇心来引导你。你想要多一些什么？少一些什么？这个岗位中是否有某些部分，点燃了你对另一条路的兴趣——产品、工程管理，还是资深技术专家（staff engineering）？

You don't need all the answers right now. But you do need to start asking the right questions and paying attention to the patterns.

你现在不需要拥有全部答案。但你确实需要开始问对的问题，并留意其中的规律。

Some people prefer consistent tracking over a single big reflection moment. Daily journaling or regular check-ins can give you a clearer picture by capturing what's true in the moment, rather than relying on memory or standout experiences. It's a more accurate way to spot patterns, like what energizes you, what drains you, and how those shifts show up day-to-day, but it does require more consistent effort.

有些人更倾向于持续记录，而不是靠某一次大型的反思时刻。每日写日志或定期自我检视，能捕捉当下真实的状态，而不是依赖记忆或那些印象深刻的经历，从而给你一幅更清晰的画面。这是发现规律——什么让你充满能量、什么耗尽你、以及这些起伏在日常中如何呈现——更准确的方式，但它确实需要更持续的投入。

Whatever approach you choose, the goal is the same: to gather the raw material for better career decisions and to honor the journey you've already taken.

无论你选择哪种方式，目标都是一样的：为更好的职业决策收集原材料，也为你已经走过的这段旅程留下一份郑重的记录。

Identify Your Strengths and Areas for Improvement as a Leader认清你作为领导者的优势与待提升之处

Once you've taken time to reflect on what you enjoy and don't enjoy about the tech lead role, the next step is to translate that reflection into clarity about your strengths and areas for growth.

当你花时间反思了自己喜欢与不喜欢技术负责人岗位的哪些方面之后，下一步就是把这份反思转化为对“自己优势与待成长之处”的清晰认识。

The better you understand your current shape as a leader, the better equipped you'll be to make thoughtful career choices and design your growth path.

你越清楚自己目前作为领导者的“形态”，就越有能力做出深思熟虑的职业选择，并设计出属于自己的成长路径。

This clarity ensures that you choose a next role that plays to your strengths. It allows you to focus your learning and development time more effectively. It helps you have more informed and confident career conversations. And it gives you the foundation to advocate for yourself and track your own progress over time.

这份清晰，能确保你选到一个能让优势充分发挥的下一份岗位；能让你更有效地把学习与发展时间用在刀刃上；能帮你在职业对话中更有依据、更有底气；也为你“主动为自己争取、并长期追踪自身进展”打下基础。

A simple way to start is by using tools like VIA Character Strengths, CliftonStrengths/StrengthsFinder, or a Work Styles Assessment. While many people are understandably skeptical of these tools, as they're not scientifically rigorous, they can still offer real value when used thoughtfully. At the very least, they prompt useful self-reflection and can surface patterns or themes you might not have noticed on your own.

一个简单的入手方式，是借助 VIA 性格优势、CliftonStrengths（优势识别器）或工作风格测评这类工具。尽管很多人对这类工具持怀疑态度也情有可原——毕竟它们在科学上并不严格——但只要用心使用，它们仍能提供真实的价值。至少，它们能触发有用的自我反思，并把你自己可能未曾留意的规律或主题浮现出来。

— PDF p.359 —

Just be mindful not to treat them as fixed truths or personality labels. These tests don't define you; the outcome is only as helpful as the insight it triggers. Focus on what resonates, discard what doesn't, and remember that context always matters: the same strength can show up very differently depending on your role, team, or environment.

只是要注意，别把它们当成一成不变的真理或人格标签。这些测评并不能定义你；结果的价值，仅仅等同于它所触发的那份洞察。留下那些与你产生共鸣的，舍弃那些不契合的，并记住：情境永远重要——同一项优势，会因你的岗位、团队或环境不同，而呈现出截然不同的样子。

Even disagreeing with the results can be eye-opening. It can help clarify how you see yourself or the kind of leader you want to become. These tools aren't definitive, but they can trigger meaningful conversations, especially with yourself.

哪怕是不认同测评结果，也可能让你眼前一亮。它能帮你厘清“你如何看待自己”，或“你想成为什么样的领导者”。这些工具并非定论，但它们能触发有意义的对话——尤其是和你自己的对话。

Use a combination of self-reflection and external input to map your strengths and gaps. Building on the insights from reflective tools and feedback, this step allows you to connect what you're learning about yourself with how others experience your impact. It bridges internal awareness with external perception, giving you a more accurate, well-rounded picture of where you currently stand and where you can grow next.

把自我反思与外部反馈结合起来，描绘出你的优势与缺口。在反思工具和反馈所带来的洞察基础上，这一步让你把“你对自己的认识”与“别人如何感受你的影响力”连接起来。它在内部觉察与外部认知之间架起桥梁，让你对“自己目前所处的位置、以及下一步可以在哪里成长”有一幅更准确、更全面的画面。

What have you consistently done well? Think about the moments when others turned to you. What were you doing? Were you mentoring, solving hard tech problems, calming things during an incident, facilitating cross-functional planning? What do people often thank you for? What do team members and stakeholders rely on you for? What types of challenges do you handle with ease?

你一直以来都把哪些事情做得不错？回想一下那些别人会来找你的时刻。当时你在做什么？是在辅导他人、攻克棘手的技术难题，还是在事故中稳住局面、主持跨职能规划？人们常常因为什么感谢你？团队成员和干系人在哪些事情上依赖你？哪一类挑战你能处理得游刃有余？

What feedback have you received? Review feedback from multiple sources, such as performance reviews, retrospectives, one-on-one check-ins, informal praise, or constructive notes from peers. Look for patterns. One comment might be an outlier, but repeated themes are signals. If you don't have feedback handy, ask. Reach out to a few trusted peers or collaborators and say, "I'm reflecting on my leadership journey. Is there anything you've noticed that I tend to do well or could do better?"

你收到过哪些反馈？回顾来自多方的反馈，比如绩效评审、回顾会、一对一沟通、非正式的表扬，或是同事们建设性的留言。去寻找规律。单条评论可能只是个例外，但反复出现的主题才是信号。如果手头没有现成的反馈，那就主动去问。联系几位你信任的同事或协作者，对他们说：“我正在反思自己的领导力成长之路。你有没有注意到，我有哪些事做得不错，或者哪些地方可以做得更好？”

What challenges have you struggled with? What drained your energy, felt consistently difficult, or led to less-than-ideal outcomes? Sometimes these are skill gaps. Other times, they signal misalignment with your natural strengths or interests. What situations leave you second-guessing yourself? Where do you often need to ask for help? What have you avoided doing, even though you knew it mattered? This isn't a moment to be self-critical; it's a moment to be curious. Why do these things feel hard? Is it something you want to get better at? Or something you want to do less of in the future?

你在哪些挑战上挣扎过？是什么耗尽了你的精力、始终让你觉得困难，或是导致了不太理想的结果？有时这些是技能缺口；另一些时候，它们预示着与你天生的优势或兴趣之间的错配。什么样的情境会让你事后反复怀疑自己？你通常在哪些地方需要求助？有哪些事你明知重要，却一直回避着不去做？这不是自我批判的时刻，而是保持好奇的时刻。这些事为什么让你觉得难？是你想变得更擅长的东西？还是你未来想少做一些的东西？

Whatever you discover in this reflection process, take a moment to celebrate. What's easier now than it was six months ago? What used to feel hard that now

无论你在这场反思中发现了什么，都花一点时间为自己庆贺。有什么事情现在比半年前更轻松了？有什么曾经觉得困难、如今

— PDF p.360 —

feels natural? Maybe you finally feel comfortable leading architecture reviews. Maybe you ran a retro that shifted how your team works. Maybe you gave feedback that landed well.

却已变得自然而然？也许你终于能从容地主持架构评审了；也许你主持的一次回顾会，改变了团队的工作方式；又或者你给出的一次反馈，恰到好处地被对方接受了。

Those are signs of growth. Write them down. They're proof of your evolution, and they'll be useful when it's time to build your growth plan for your next move. (More on building a growth plan in the section "Developing a Personal Growth Plan" on page 38.)

这些都是成长的迹象。把它们写下来。它们是你蜕变的证明，在你为下一步制定成长计划时会很有用。（关于如何制定成长计划，详见第 38 页“制定个人成长计划”一节。）

Possible Career Paths After Tech Lead技术负责人之后的可能职业路径

Once you've taken the time to reflect on your experience as a tech lead—what energizes you, what challenges you, and where your strengths lie—the next natural question is: where do I go from here?

当你花时间反思过自己作为技术负责人的经历——什么让你充满能量、什么让你感到挑战、以及你的优势在哪里——接下来那个自然而然的问题就是：从这里出发，我该往哪走？

The good news is, there's no single path forward. The tech lead role sits at a unique crossroads between technical depth, people leadership, and organizational influence, and from here, your next step can take many forms.

好消息是：前方并没有一条唯一的路。技术负责人这个岗位，正处在技术深度、人员领导力与组织影响力三者交汇的独特路口；从这里出发，你的下一步可以呈现出许多种形态。

Some tech leads transition into engineering manager roles and focus more on people and team development. Others lean into technical mastery by stepping into Staff+ or architect roles. Some shift toward coordination and execution as technical program managers, and a few even branch out into consulting or advisory work, bringing their experience to a broader set of teams.

有些技术负责人转型为工程经理（EM），把重心更多放在人员与团队发展上；另一些人则走向技术精通，迈入 Staff+ 或架构师岗位；还有一些人转向协调与执行，成为技术项目经理（TPM）；少数人甚至拓展到咨询或顾问工作，把自己的经验带给更广泛的团队。

In this section, I'll explore these options: what each path looks like, what types of people tend to thrive in them, and how to recognize which might be right for you.

在本节里，我会逐一探讨这些选项：每条路径长什么样、哪类人往往在其中如鱼得水，以及如何辨认出哪一条可能适合你。

Advancing to Engineering Manager晋升为工程经理

If you found yourself enjoying the people side of the role while reflecting on your experience as a tech lead, then a transition to the EM role might feel like a natural next step. In fact, it's one of the most common career moves after being a tech lead. The EM path is especially suited for those who are energized by growing people, shaping team culture, and influencing broader organizational direction.

如果你在反思技术负责人经历时，发现自己享受的是这个岗位中“与人打交道”的那一面，那么转型到工程经理（EM）岗位，可能会感觉像一个顺理成章的下一步。事实上，这是技术负责人之后最常见的职业路径之一。EM 这条路尤其适合那些“因培养人、塑造团队文化、影响更宏观的组织方向而充满能量”的人。

Before I go into describing what the EM role is and how it's different from the tech lead role, it's important to mention: just as there is a lot of confusion around the tech lead role in the industry, the same is true, though perhaps less talked about, for the EM role. While EMs typically sit one level higher in the organizational hierarchy, the debates that surround the tech lead role also show up here: How technical should an EM be? How hands-on? How involved should they be in day-to-day team operations?

在我描述 EM 岗位究竟是什么、以及它与技术负责人有何不同之前，有一点必须先说明：正如行业里对技术负责人这个角色充满困惑一样，EM 岗位也是如此——只是谈论得相对少一些。虽然 EM 在组织层级上通常高一级，但围绕技术负责人的那些争论，在这里同样会出现：一个 EM 该多懂技术？该多亲力亲为？该在多大程度上介入团队的日常运作？

— PDF p.361 —

The answers vary widely. The definition of the EM role depends heavily on how many teams they manage, whether those teams already have tech leads, and the broader structure of the organization. When teams are missing strong tech leads, the EM often ends up pulled into more technical or operational detail than is ideal.

答案五花八门。EM 岗位的定义，很大程度上取决于他们管理多少个团队、这些团队是否已经有技术负责人，以及组织的整体架构。当团队缺少强有力的技术负责人时，EM 往往会被拉进过多本不该由他负责的技术或运营细节中。

My personal take is similar to how I view the tech lead role: the EM role should be a highly people-focused one. But that view usually works better under a specific setup, one I've seen succeed repeatedly in my experience. In this setup, each team has a strong tech lead, and the EM works closely with them, focusing on the broader organizational view, people development, and long-term team health. Ideally, an EM supports multiple teams, allowing a clear separation between the responsibilities of EMs and tech leads.

我个人的看法，与我对技术负责人岗位的看法类似：EM 应当是一个高度聚焦于人的角色。但这种看法通常只在一种特定配置下才更奏效——而这种配置，是我在实践中反复看到它成功的。在这种配置里，每个团队都有一位强有力的技术负责人，EM 与他们紧密协作，把精力放在更宏观的组织视角、人员发展和团队长期健康上。理想情况下，一位 EM 支持多个团队，从而让 EM 与技术负责人的职责之间有一道清晰的分界。

In my experience, any extreme, whether it's having no tech leads at all, only EMs managing multiple teams, or having every tech lead report directly to the head of engineering, can quickly become overwhelming and unsustainable. I once consulted for a startup that had no tech leads, just EMs overseeing several teams. One EM was responsible for three different teams and was constantly pulled between technical decisions and people management. She was excellent at her job but visibly overworked. It was clear the absence of tech leads was creating unnecessary strain, both for her and for the teams that lacked day-to-day technical leadership.

以我的经验，任何极端做法——无论是完全不设技术负责人、只由 EM 来管好几个团队，还是让每位技术负责人都直接向工程负责人汇报——都很快会变得不堪重负、难以为继。我曾为一家初创公司做咨询，那里没有技术负责人，只有 EM 在统管好几个团队。有一位 EM 负责三个不同的团队，整天在技术决策和人员管理之间被来回拉扯。她业务能力极强，但明显已经过劳。很明显，技术负责人的缺位，正在给她本人、以及那些缺少日常技术领导的团队，都造成不必要的压力。

Of course, there are many functioning org structures out there with different formats. That doesn't make one model better than another, just different.

当然，市面上存在着许多运转良好、形态各异的组织架构。这并不意味着某一种模式就比另一种更好，只是不同而已。

It's also worth noting a current trend in the industry. At the time of writing, particularly with the AI boom, more and more EMs are expected to be close to the code and even to be contributing regularly. Personally, I disagree with this expectation. I don't believe EMs should be required to write production code. In fact, I think an EM coding outside of a team's regular process can do more harm than good. There are better ways for an EM to use their technical expertise: participating in high-level architectural decisions, helping with planning and expectation management, supporting tech leads, and ensuring long-term technical sustainability.

另外值得一提的是行业里当下的一个趋势。在撰写本书时，尤其是在 AI 热潮之下，越来越多的 EM 被要求贴近代码、甚至定期亲自贡献代码。就我个人而言，我并不认同这种期待。我不认为 EM 应该被要求去写生产代码。事实上，我认为一个 EM 跳出团队常规流程去写代码，往往弊大于利。EM 有更好的方式来发挥自己的技术专长：参与高层架构决策、协助做规划与预期管理、支持技术负责人，以及确保技术上的长期可持续性。

That said, I'm open to being proven wrong. Each company and team operates differently, and sometimes experimentation leads to surprising results. But as a default, I advocate for a hands-off EM model, one rooted in trust, strategic thinking, and team enablement.

话虽如此，我也乐于被证明是错的。每家公司、每个团队的运作方式都不同，有时实验会带来令人惊喜的结果。但作为一种默认主张，我推崇“放手式”的 EM 模式——一种根植于信任、战略思考与团队赋能的模式。

So, what does the EM role actually look like in practice?

那么，EM 这个岗位在实际工作中究竟是什么样子？

— PDF p.362 —

Based on the points I outlined earlier, the key differences between the tech lead and EM roles fall into a few major categories.

基于我前面提到的几点，技术负责人与 EM 之间的关键差异，可以归纳为几大类。

First, the level of influence. EMs typically sit one level higher in the organizational hierarchy, which gives them access to more upper leadership, broader visibility, and earlier awareness of company-wide changes. They're often included in planning conversations that shape future direction months in advance—things tech leads may learn about only once they begin impacting delivery.

第一，是影响力的层级。EM 在组织层级上通常高一级，这让他们能接触到更上层的领导、拥有更宽的可见度，并更早地获悉全公司范围的变动。他们常常参与那些提前数月就决定未来方向的规划讨论——而这些事，技术负责人往往要等到开始影响交付时才会听说。

In addition, the nature of stakeholder relationships shifts. While tech leads primarily collaborate with their immediate team and cross-functional partners like product, design, and their EM, engineering managers engage with a broader and more senior set of stakeholders, including HR, finance, other EMs, and senior leadership. The stakes are also higher: conversations often center on resourcing, organizational design, business risk, and long-term strategy. As a result, EMs must adopt an even more business-oriented communication style, framing decisions in terms of impact, return on investment, and alignment with company objectives.

此外，干系人关系的性质也发生了变化。技术负责人主要与自己的直接团队以及产品、设计、本团队 EM 等跨职能伙伴协作；而工程经理面对的，则是一批更广泛、也更资深的干系人——包括 HR、财务、其他 EM 以及高层领导。筹码也更高：谈话常常围绕资源配置、组织设计、业务风险和长期战略展开。因此，EM 必须采用一种更加业务导向的沟通方式，用“影响力、投资回报率、与公司目标是否一致”来框定决策。

Second, the scope of involvement. A tech lead should focus deeply on a single team, working closely with engineers in the day-to-day, guiding technical decisions, and unblocking delivery. An EM, by contrast, may support multiple teams. That broader scope means they're less embedded in any one team's daily challenges and more focused on patterns, people dynamics, and long-term team health across the board.

第二，是参与的范围。技术负责人应当深度聚焦于单个团队，与工程师们在日常中紧密协作，指导技术决策、为交付扫清障碍。相比之下，一位 EM 可能要支持多个团队。这种更宽的范围意味着：他们不会深陷于某一个团队的日常挑战，而是更关注整体层面的规律、人的互动动态，以及各个团队的长期健康。

Third, decision-making power. While tech leads often provide input on things like performance reviews, compensation, and growth opportunities, EMs usually make the final calls. They're the ones responsible for promotions, salary changes, budget allocation, and sometimes having tough conversations around underperformance. A strong tech lead will guide and support their team members closely, but it's often the EM who formalizes and delivers the outcomes.

第三，是决策的权力。技术负责人常常在绩效评审、薪酬和成长机会等事情上提供意见，而 EM 通常才是拍板的人。晋升、调薪、预算分配，有时还有围绕绩效不佳的艰难谈话，都由他们负责。一位得力的技术负责人会密切引导和支持团队成员，但把结果正式确定下来、并传达下去的，往往是 EM。

Finally, there's a difference in relationship dynamics. Tech leads are in frequent one-on-ones with their team members; those conversations are core to the role. With EMs, one-on-ones with individual engineers might be less frequent, especially when teams have active tech leads. Instead, EMs are likely to have more regular syncs with tech leads themselves, supporting them in supporting the team.

最后，是关系互动上的差异。技术负责人与团队成员之间有频繁的一对一沟通，这些谈话是这个岗位的核心。而对 EM 来说，与单个工程师的一对一会谈可能没那么频繁——尤其是当团队已经有活跃的技术负责人时。取而代之的，是 EM 更可能与技术负责人本人定期同步，通过支持他们来支持整个团队。

So the real question is: are you ready to move even further away from the code?

所以真正的问题是：你准备好离代码更远一些了吗？

— PDF p.363 —

If yes, the EM path might be a great fit. But if you feel more fulfilled working through complex technical challenges yourself and staying closer to the code, you may want to explore staff engineer or architect paths instead, which I'll cover next.

如果答案是肯定的，那么 EM 这条路可能非常适合你。但如果你更享受自己亲手攻克复杂的技术挑战、愿意离代码更近一些，那你也许该转而探索资深工程师（staff engineer）或架构师的路径——这正是我接下来要讲的。

Specializing as a Staff+ or Architect走专业路线：Staff+ 工程师或架构师

If the EM role doesn't sound like a fit—maybe you're not drawn to managing people's development, handling performance reviews, or distributing budgets—and you'd prefer to remain on the technical track, then a Staff+ role, such as staff engineer or architect, might be a better path moving forward. These roles allow you to stay close to the technology, focus on complex engineering challenges (driving major infrastructure migrations, solving critical reliability issues), and lead through technical expertise rather than through direct management.

如果 EM 岗位听起来并不适合你——也许你并不向往去管理别人的成长、处理绩效评审或分配预算——而你更愿意留在技术这条轨道上，那么一个 Staff+ 岗位，比如资深工程师或架构师，可能是更合适的前进方向。这些岗位让你能贴近技术，专注于复杂的工程挑战（主导大型基础设施迁移、解决关键的可靠性问题），并通过技术专长而非直接的人员管理来发挥领导力。

Note that when I refer to Staff+, I'm talking about the family of senior individual contributor roles that typically include titles like staff engineer, senior staff, principal engineer, and distinguished engineer. While the naming and levels vary across companies, what they share is a common idea: as you progress through these levels, your influence grows from the team level, to multiple teams, and eventually to the organization as a whole. With each step, the expectation is that your impact increases accordingly—not just through individual contributions but through broader technical leadership.

请注意，当我说到 Staff+ 时，指的是那一族高级个人贡献者岗位，通常包括资深工程师（staff engineer）、高级资深工程师（senior staff）、主任工程师（principal engineer）和杰出工程师（distinguished engineer）等头衔。虽然各家公司的命名与级别各不相同，但它们共享同一个理念：随着你在这些级别上晋升，你的影响力会从团队层面，扩展到多个团队，并最终扩展到整个组织。每上一个台阶，对你的期待都是影响力随之提升——而且不仅仅是通过个人贡献，更是通过更宏观的技术领导力。

Just like with the tech lead role, there are varying opinions and definitions out there for what these roles entail. To explain the range of perspectives, I'll reference a few voices that have articulated them clearly.

就像技术负责人岗位一样，对于这些岗位究竟意味着什么，外界也存在着五花八门的看法与定义。为了把这种观点的光谱讲清楚，我会引用几位把它们阐释得很透彻的作者。

There are a few defining traits that the Staff+ and architect roles have in common, starting with "You're not a manager, but you are a leader." This is one of the key takeaways from Tanya Reilly's The Staff Engineer's Path, and it applies just as much to architects as it does to staff engineers. Even without direct reports or formal managerial authority, these roles come with expectations of high impact, maturity, and influence.

Staff+ 与架构师岗位有几个共同的决定性特征，首先一条就是：“你不是经理，但你是一位领导者。”这是 Tanya Reilly 在《资深工程师之路》（The Staff Engineer's Path）中给出的核心观点之一，它既适用于资深工程师，也同样适用于架构师。即便没有直接下属、没有正式的管理职权，这些岗位本身就伴随着对“高影响力、成熟度与影响力”的期待。

Reilly puts it clearly: "Staff engineers lead differently than managers…. Their impact happens in other ways." Staff engineers are expected to be the grown-ups in the room: calm in a crisis, grounded in judgment, and trusted to lead without needing authority. Their leadership shows up not in performance reviews or approving time off but in how they shape systems, mentor team members, make technical calls, and guide the team through complexity.

Reilly 说得很明白：“资深工程师的领导方式与经理不同……他们的影响力以另一种方式发生。”资深工程师被期待成为房间里那个“成熟可靠的人”：危机中保持冷静、判断脚踏实地、无需职权也能被信任去带队。他们的领导力，不体现在绩效评审或审批请假上，而体现在他们如何塑造系统、辅导团队成员、做出技术决策，并带领团队穿越复杂性。

At this level, technical expertise is just the foundation. You're also expected to influence cross-team decisions, align with business needs, and communicate

在这个级别上，技术专长仅仅是地基。你还被期待去影响跨团队的决策、对齐业务需求，并与

— PDF p.364 —

clearly with diverse audiences. Besides deep technical skills, these roles demand collaboration, teaching, and strategic thinking.

形形色色的受众进行清晰的沟通。除了深厚的技术功底，这些岗位还要求协作能力、教学能力和战略思考。

This aligns with the view of leadership described by Will Larson in his article "Staff Archetypes": leadership can look like mentoring, shaping patterns, influencing without authority, and raising the quality bar across the board.

这与 Will Larson 在其文章《资深工程师原型》（"Staff Archetypes"）中描述的领导力观是一致的：领导力可以体现为辅导他人、塑造范式、在没有职权的情况下施加影响，以及全面抬高质量的标准线。

The main differences between staff engineer and architect roles tend to center on scope, visibility, and approach.

资深工程师与架构师之间的主要差异，往往集中在范围、可见度和工作方式上。

Staff engineers are typically embedded within one or a small number of teams, where they focus on high-impact technical work. They're deeply involved in day-to-day engineering challenges, reviewing designs, writing code, mentoring peers, and unblocking complexity as it arises. They're often seen as domain owners: the go-to experts for a specific technical area.

资深工程师通常嵌入在一个或少数几个团队之中，专注于高影响力的技术工作。他们深度参与日常的工程挑战——评审设计、编写代码、辅导同事，并在复杂性出现时为之拆解扫除。他们往往被视为某个领域的主人（domain owner）：某个特定技术领域里“遇事必问”的专家。

In smaller or less mature organizations, these responsibilities can overlap with those of a senior engineer. The key difference often comes down to scope, influence, and consistency of impact. While a senior engineer might lead a project within the team's scope, a staff engineer is expected to lead across boundaries, influencing technical direction beyond their immediate team and operating with a broader, more strategic lens.

在较小或不太成熟的组织里，这些职责可能与高级工程师重叠。关键的差别，往往归结为范围、影响力以及影响力的持续性。高级工程师可能只是在团队范围之内牵头一个项目；而资深工程师则被期待跨边界去引领，把技术方向的影响扩展到自己的直接团队之外，并用一种更宏观、更具战略意味的视角来运作。

Architects, on the other hand, tend to operate across multiple teams or even entire departments. They define system boundaries, maintain architectural consistency, and guide long-term evolution across projects. They focus more on big-picture design, scalability, and aligning technology strategy with business goals.

而架构师，则往往在多个团队、甚至整个部门之间开展工作。他们定义系统边界、维护架构的一致性，并指导跨项目的长期演进。他们更关注大局设计、可扩展性，以及让技术战略与业务目标对齐。

Will Larson describes the architect role as an archetype of the staff engineer role. In his view, architects are responsible for the success of a particular technical domain, such as cloud infrastructure or API design, and that domain must be complex and central enough to justify this kind of specialized ownership. He also counters the negative stereotype of architects working in isolation. Effective architects, he says, are embedded in the business context and earn influence through judgment and collaboration.

Will Larson 把架构师岗位描述为资深工程师岗位的一种原型。在他看来，架构师要为某个特定技术领域——比如云基础设施或 API 设计——的成功负责，而这个领域必须足够复杂、足够核心，才配得上这种专门化的“主人翁”角色。他也反驳了“架构师闭门造车”这种负面刻板印象。他说，高效的架构师是嵌入在业务语境之中的，他们通过判断力和协作来赢得影响力。

Another key difference is how hands-on the role remains. Staff engineers are expected to be close to the codebase, while architect expectations vary by organization. Some companies expect architects to write code regularly; others want them focused on design and alignment. Both models can work; what matters is clarity on the expectations and a good match between the role and your strengths.

另一个关键差异，在于这个岗位还保留多少“动手”的成分。资深工程师被期待贴近代码库，而对架构师的期待则因组织而异。有些公司希望架构师定期写代码；另一些公司则希望他们专注于设计与对齐。两种模式都行得通；重要的是对“期待是什么”有清晰的认识，并让这个岗位与你的优势良好匹配。

— PDF p.365 —

So how are these roles different from the tech lead role? Think of the tech lead as sitting somewhere between the people-focused EM and the technically deep staff engineer or architect. Tech leads are often responsible for delivery within a single team, balancing both technical guidance and day-to-day coordination. In contrast, Staff+ and architect roles lean much more deeply into the technical end of the spectrum. They're expected to drive technical direction across teams, lead through influence, and solve large-scale engineering problems without managing people directly.

那么，这些岗位与技术负责人岗位又有何不同？可以把技术负责人想象成处在“聚焦于人的 EM”与“技术精深的资深工程师或架构师”之间的某个位置。技术负责人通常负责单个团队内部的交付，在技术指导与日常协调之间左右平衡。相比之下，Staff+ 与架构师岗位，则更加深入地偏向光谱的技术一端。他们被期待在跨团队层面推动技术方向、通过影响力来带队，并在不直接管理人员的前提下解决大规模的工程问题。

So if you want to go even deeper into technology, and you enjoy leading through influence, design, and problem-solving more than through people management, Staff+ or architect paths might be a strong fit. For many, it's an ideal way to stay rooted in technical work while continuing to grow their impact across the organization.

所以，如果你想在技术上走得更深，并且比起通过人员管理来带队，你更享受通过影响力、设计和解决问题来引领，那么 Staff+ 或架构师路径可能非常适合你。对许多人来说，这是一种理想的方式：既让自己扎根于技术工作，又能持续扩大自己在整个组织中的影响力。

Transitioning to a Technical Program Manager Role转型为技术项目经理（TPM）

If, as a tech lead, you found yourself energized by driving alignment across teams, navigating complex project scopes, or orchestrating delivery plans but felt less attached to deep technical ownership or hands-on coding, the technical program manager (TPM) path might be a natural evolution.

如果你作为技术负责人时，发现自己因“推动跨团队对齐、驾驭复杂的项目范围、统筹交付计划”而充满能量，却对“深度的技术主人翁责任或亲手写代码”没那么留恋，那么技术项目经理（TPM）这条路，可能是一种顺理成章的演进。

TPMs are responsible for managing large-scale, cross-functional initiatives that require coordination across engineering, product, design, and business teams. Their superpower is anticipating risk, aligning stakeholders, managing dependencies, and keeping delivery on track, especially in fast-moving or high-complexity environments.

TPM 负责管理大规模、跨职能的项目，这类项目需要在工程、产品、设计和业务团队之间进行协调。他们的“超能力”在于：预判风险、对齐干系人、管理依赖关系，并让交付始终走在正轨上——尤其是在节奏快、复杂度高的环境里。

While they're not expected to code, TPMs typically have strong technical backgrounds. This technical fluency helps them understand trade-offs, ask the right questions, and connect the dots between engineering decisions and business goals. In many ways, a former tech lead stepping into a TPM role already has a head start: you're used to operating at the intersection of technology, product, and execution.

虽然 TPM 不被要求写代码，但他们通常具备扎实的技术背景。这种技术上的纯熟，帮他们理解取舍、问出恰当的问题，并把工程决策与业务目标之间的点点线线连接起来。从很多方面看，一位前技术负责人转岗做 TPM 本来就占得先机：你早已习惯在技术、产品与执行三者的交汇处开展工作。

TPMs shine in situations where the scope spans multiple teams or systems, where aligning various stakeholders on timing and outcomes is critical, where coordination costs are high or timelines are long, and where product and engineering teams need structured delivery support.

在以下情境中，TPM 尤其能大放异彩：项目范围横跨多个团队或系统；在时间节点与结果上对齐各方干系人命悬一线；协调成本高昂或周期漫长；以及产品与工程团队需要结构化的交付支持。

One important distinction: while TPMs often collaborate closely with engineering managers and tech leads, their focus is more on program execution than people development or system architecture. That said, strong TPMs bring

有一点重要的区别：虽然 TPM 常常与工程经理和技术负责人紧密协作，但他们的焦点更偏向项目执行，而非人员发展或系统架构。话虽如此，出色的 TPM 会为那些

— PDF p.366 —

leadership, clarity, and calm to situations where ambiguity is high and stakes are even higher.

“模糊度很高、而筹码更高”的局面，带来领导力、清晰度与从容。

If you enjoy steering planning sessions, solving organizational blockers, and being the glue across teams but don't feel the pull to manage people or deepen your technical specialization, the TPM role can offer high impact and visibility, without requiring a move into traditional management or staying deep in the code.

如果你喜欢主持规划会议、清除组织上的障碍、做跨团队之间那道“黏合剂”，却并不向往去管理人员，也不想深耕技术专业化，那么 TPM 岗位能带给你高影响力与高可见度，而无需你转入传统的管理轨道，也不必深陷代码之中。

Getting into Consulting or Advisory Roles进入咨询或顾问岗位

If you've developed strong expertise as a tech lead and enjoy solving complex problems across a variety of contexts, a move into consulting or advisory work could be a compelling next step. These roles let you apply your knowledge more broadly, often across multiple teams, organizations, or industries, without being tied to a single delivery team or company structure.

如果你作为技术负责人已经练就了扎实的专长，并且享受在各种不同情境下解决复杂问题，那么转入咨询或顾问工作，可能是一个很有吸引力的下一步。这些岗位让你能把知识运用到更广阔的范围——常常横跨多个团队、组织或行业——而不必被绑死在某一个交付团队或公司架构上。

Consultants are typically brought in to provide clarity, solve thorny problems, or accelerate transformation. You might be asked to evaluate architecture, improve delivery practices, or help a struggling team level up its ways of working. Advisory roles are similar but often longer-term and more strategic, and sometimes at the executive level, helping organizations make high-impact technical or organizational decisions.

顾问（consultant）通常是被请来提供清晰度、解决棘手问题，或是加速转型的。你可能会被邀请去评估架构、改进交付实践，或是帮助一个陷入困境的团队提升其工作方式。顾问（advisory）岗位与此类似，但往往更长期、更具战略意味，有时还处于高管层面，帮助组织做出高影响力的技术或组织决策。

This path is a great fit if you enjoy stepping into messy situations, quickly making sense of unfamiliar systems, and having a bird's-eye view of how different parts of a business connect. It's also a good option if you want more flexibility or autonomy in your work, as many consultants and advisors work independently or in smaller specialized firms.

如果你喜欢一头扎进乱糟糟的局面、迅速摸清陌生系统，并对“业务的各个部分如何连接起来”拥有鸟瞰式的视野，那么这条路会非常适合你。如果你希望工作中有更多灵活性或自主权，它也是一个不错的选择——因为许多顾问和咨询师都是独立工作，或是在小型的专业公司里工作。

But it's not for everyone. Consulting requires high adaptability, strong communication skills, and a certain level of emotional intelligence. You'll often be an outsider, so building trust quickly is critical. You also need to be comfortable with ambiguity and able to deliver value without always having full control over execution.

但它并不适合所有人。咨询工作要求高度的适应力、出色的沟通技巧，以及一定程度的情商。你常常是个“外来者”，所以能否快速建立信任至关重要。你还需要能与模糊共处，并在并不总能完全掌控执行的情况下，依然交付价值。

Still, for experienced tech leads who want variety, influence, and the chance to work across broader scopes, consulting or advisory roles can offer rich and meaningful ways to grow their careers.

尽管如此，对于那些渴望变化、影响力以及在更广阔范围里施展的资深技术负责人来说，咨询或顾问岗位能为他们的职业成长提供丰富而有意义的路径。

Take my own journey as an example. After working as a tech lead at Thoughtworks, I transitioned into being a full-time consultant, trainer, and career coach. I realized that the skills I had built over the years, from mentoring and stakeholder management to systems thinking and communication, could bring value in different forms beyond a single team or company.

以我自己的经历为例。在 Thoughtworks 担任技术负责人之后，我转型成为一名全职的顾问、培训师和职业教练。我意识到，这些年来练就的技能——从辅导他人、干系人管理，到系统思考与沟通——完全可以在单个团队或公司之外，以不同的形态带来价值。

— PDF p.367 —

Over the past four years, I've coached more than 500 professionals across levels and disciplines, trained over 300 tech leads on building high-performing teams, and worked with a number of companies to improve engineering practices and leadership culture. I've also built a community of nearly 30,000 people by sharing stories and lessons learned on LinkedIn and through my newsletter.

在过去四年里，我辅导了 500 多位来自不同级别、不同专业的职场人，培训了 300 多位技术负责人如何打造高绩效团队，并与多家公司合作改进工程实践与领导力文化。我还通过在 LinkedIn 上、以及通过我的通讯分享故事与经验教训，建立起一个近三万人的社群。

I share this not to position my path as the path but to highlight that the tech lead role often prepares you for more than you realize. It can be a powerful springboard into a wide variety of roles or even portfolio careers that align better with your goals and values over time.

我分享这些，并不是要把我的路说成唯一的路，而是想强调：技术负责人这个岗位，往往为你准备的东西比你意识到的要多。它可以成为一块强有力的跳板，带你跳向各种各样的岗位，甚至是“组合式职业”（portfolio career）——随着时间推移，后者能与你的目标和价值观更好地契合。

The key takeaway: the skills you're developing now—solving problems, growing people, aligning stakeholders, communicating clearly—are valuable well beyond your current title. You may be closer than you think to your next career move.

关键的收获在于：你此刻正在打磨的那些技能——解决问题、培养人、对齐干系人、清晰沟通——其价值远远超出你眼下的头衔。也许，你离自己的下一次职业跨越，比你想象的更近。

Planning Your Transition规划你的转型

Once you've identified a direction that feels aligned with your strengths and interests, the next step is turning that vision into action. Career growth doesn't happen all at once; it happens through intentional choices, small experiments, and clear preparation.

一旦你找到了一个与自己优势和兴趣相契合的方向，下一步就是把这份愿景转化为行动。职业成长不是一蹴而就的；它是通过有意识的选择、小小的实验和清晰的准备，一步步发生的。

Whether you're aiming to become an engineering manager, a Staff+ engineer, a TPM, or something else entirely, the way you approach the transition matters. This section is about helping you bridge the gap between where you are and where you want to be.

无论你的目标是成为工程经理、Staff+ 工程师、TPM，还是全然不同的什么岗位，你对待这次转型的方式都很重要。本节的主旨，就是帮你在“你现在所在的位置”与“你想去的位置”之间架起一座桥。

I'll talk about how to choose your next step with intention, how to prepare yourself for the shift (mentally, emotionally, and practically), and why it's OK if your path isn't linear. Most importantly, I'll remind you that you're not locked in, and you have more flexibility than you think.

我会谈谈如何有意识地选择下一步、如何为这次转变做好准备（心理上、情感上和实操上），以及为什么你的路径即使不是一条直线也完全没关系。最重要的是，我会提醒你：你并非被锁死在一条路上，你拥有的灵活性比你以为的要多。

Choose Your Next Step with Intention有意识地选择下一步

Now that you've reflected on what energizes you, where you thrive, and the kind of impact you want to have, it's time to make a conscious choice. Whether you feel drawn to people leadership, technical depth, strategic coordination, or advisory work, what matters most is that your next step aligns with your values and aspirations.

既然你已经反思过什么让你充满能量、你在哪里如鱼得水、以及你想产生怎样的影响，现在就是做出清醒选择的时候了。无论你被人员领导力、技术深度、战略协调还是顾问工作所吸引，最重要的是：你的下一步要与你的价值观和志向相一致。

You don't need to have everything figured out. What's important is that you're moving forward with self-awareness and curiosity, not just following the default path. Your time as a tech lead has given you insight into what you

你不需要把一切都想清楚。重要的是，你是带着自我觉察和好奇心向前走，而不只是顺着默认路径随波逐流。你担任技术负责人的这段时光，已经让你看清楚自己

— PDF p.368 —

enjoy, where you make the biggest impact, and where you want to grow. Let that learning guide your next move.

享受什么、在哪里产生最大的影响，以及你想在哪里成长。让这些洞察来指引你的下一步。

That reflection sets the foundation. Now it's time to prepare for the shift.

这份反思打下了地基。现在，是为转变做准备的时候了。

Prepare for the Shift为转变做好准备

No transition happens overnight. Once you've gained clarity about the role you want next, the real work begins: identifying the skills, experiences, or relationships you need to develop and starting to take intentional steps toward them.

任何转型都不会一夜之间发生。一旦你想清楚了下一份想要的岗位，真正的工作才刚开始：识别出你需要去培养的技能、经历或人脉，并开始朝它们迈出有意识的步伐。

Sometimes, that means changing what you prioritize. I was once coaching a tech lead who wanted to become an engineering manager. She had a clear long-term goal, but her day-to-day choices didn't reflect it. She was deeply focused on her own team, spending most of her time coding and supporting them directly, and rarely engaging beyond that. In her words, she would "default to contributing to a feature over joining a cross-team conversation."

有时候，这意味着改变你所优先考虑的东西。我曾辅导过一位技术负责人，她想成为工程经理。她有一个清晰的长期目标，但她日常的选择却并不反映这个目标。她深度聚焦于自己的团队，把大部分时间花在写代码和直接支持团队上，很少越出这个范围去参与。用她自己的话说，她会“默认选择去为某个功能写代码，而不是加入一场跨团队的讨论”。

When she realized that her current behavior wasn't aligned with her future aspirations, she shifted her approach. She made a plan: reach out to other engineering managers, build relationships, and get involved in cross-team initiatives. This meant stepping back from some coding and resisting the urge to jump into execution mode every time the team hit a bump.

当她意识到自己当下的行为与未来的志向并不一致时，她调整了做法。她制定了一个计划：主动去联系其他工程经理、建立关系，并参与跨团队的项目。这意味着她要从一部分编码中抽身出来，并抵制住那种“每次团队一遇到坎就跳进执行模式”的冲动。

It was hard at first. She struggled with guilt about "not being helpful" or "not contributing enough." But the more we revisited her goal, reviewed how she spent her time, and talked through why this shift mattered, the easier it became to stay on track. Over time, her habits aligned more closely with her ambitions, and she started to see real progress.

起初这并不容易。她一直被一种“自己没帮上忙”或“贡献得不够多”的内疚感所困扰。但我们越是反复回顾她的目标、审视她如何花时间、并讨论这次转变为何重要，她就越容易坚持在轨道上。久而久之，她的习惯与她的志向越来越一致，她也开始看到真实的进展。

If you're preparing for a transition, here are a few ways to start:

如果你正在为一次转型做准备，下面是几个可以入手的方式：

Start by auditing your own calendar先审计你自己的日程

Inspired by the preceding story, take a look at how you've spent your time over the last one or two weeks. What types of activities are taking up most of your energy? Are they aligned with the role you're aiming for?

受上面这个故事的启发，不妨回看一下过去一两周你是如何花时间的。哪类活动占用了你大部分的精力？它们与你瞄准的那个岗位是否一致？

This kind of audit can help you spot where your time and attention are going and whether your current behavior supports your long-term goals. If not, it's a good starting point for change.

这种审计能帮你看清：你的时间和注意力都流向了哪里，以及你当下的行为是否在支撑你的长期目标。如果不一致，那它就是改变的一个很好的起点。

Make a growth plan toward the role you want为你想要的岗位制定成长计划

Start writing down the steps you need to take to reach your next role. Define the skills that qualify someone for that position, and reflect on which of those you already have and which you might need to develop.

开始把你为了抵达下一个岗位所需采取的步骤写下来。定义清楚：要胜任那个岗位，需要具备哪些技能；再反思一下，其中哪些你已经具备，哪些你可能还需要去培养。

Identify people around you who can help you get there and start building

找出你身边那些能帮你抵达目标的人，并开始建立

— PDF p.369 —

those relationships. The section "Developing a Personal Growth Plan" on page 38 covers more on how to do this effectively for the tech lead role, but the principles can be applied to any role.

这些关系。第 38 页“制定个人成长计划”一节，更详细地讲了如何针对技术负责人岗位有效地做到这一点，但这些原则同样可以应用于任何岗位。

Start having conversations开始与人交谈

One simple thing that's often overlooked: if you have clarity about where you want to go, don't keep it to yourself. Tell the people who can support or influence your next step.

有一件简单、却常被忽视的事：如果你已经清楚自己想去哪里，别把它闷在心里。告诉那些能够支持或影响你下一步的人。

Start with your manager. Many people feel like it's not OK to speak up, but great managers are usually relieved and grateful when you do. It makes their job easier: no need to dig, guess, or push. They can focus on helping you grow in the direction you actually want.

从你的经理开始。很多人觉得“说出来不太合适”，但优秀的经理在你开口时，通常会松一口气、并心存感激。这让他们的工作更轻松：不用去挖、去猜、去推。他们可以专注于帮你朝着你真正想去的方向成长。

Talk to people who are already in the role you're aiming for. Ask about their day-to-day work, their biggest challenges, and the skills they rely on most. Try questions like "What surprised you most about the role?," "What do you wish you'd known before stepping into it?," "What should someone focus on when preparing for this kind of work?" Pay attention to the patterns that emerge, especially around what strengths you already have and where you might want to grow.

去和那些已经身处你所瞄准岗位的人聊聊。问问他们日常的工作、他们最大的挑战，以及他们最依赖的技能。可以试试这样的问题：“这个岗位最让你意外的是什么？”“在接手之前，你希望自己早知道些什么？”“在为这类工作做准备时，应该重点关注什么？”留意其中浮现出来的规律，尤其是围绕“你已经具备哪些优势”以及“你可能想在哪里成长”这些部分。

And finally: tell anyone who's asking. If someone opens the door, even casually, take the opportunity to share what you're aiming for. You never know who might help open the next one.

最后一点：告诉任何一个主动问起的人。如果有人打开了一道门——哪怕只是随口一问——抓住机会分享你正在瞄准的目标。你永远不知道，谁会帮你打开下一扇门。

Shadow or partner影子学习或搭档练习

Find opportunities to work with people in the role you're aiming for. This can mean joining a project they're leading, sitting in on their planning sessions, or even just grabbing coffee to hear about their experiences. If possible, try to build a relationship with a mentor who already holds the role you're interested in. Having someone inside the company who understands the expectations, challenges, and opportunities can be incredibly valuable. They can help you gain visibility, recommend you for stretch opportunities, and offer feedback that accelerates your growth. Don't just look for someone to share tips; seek out someone who can champion your growth and help create real opportunities for you.

找机会和那些身处你所瞄准岗位的人一起工作。这可以是加入一个他们牵头的项目、旁听他们的规划会议，甚至只是约杯咖啡、听他们讲讲自己的经历。如果可能，试着与一位已经担任你所感兴趣岗位的导师建立关系。在公司内部有一位“懂行”的人——了解这个岗位的期待、挑战和机会——可能价值连城。他们能帮你获得可见度、推荐你去承担有挑战的机会，并给出能加速你成长的反馈。不要只找一个“给你支招”的人；要去找一个能为你的成长撑腰、并帮你创造真实机会的人。

Say yes to an initiative that aligns with your next step主动承接与下一步方向一致的项目

This could mean leading a cross-functional project, mentoring someone outside your team, or taking the lead in planning discussions that span teams.

这可以是牵头一个跨职能项目、辅导一位团队之外的人，或是在跨团队的规划讨论中担任主导。

— PDF p.370 —

If you want to move toward a more technical role, look for opportunities where you can demonstrate architectural thinking or contribute to system design. If you're more interested in a people leadership path like engineering management, seek coordination roles, mentor more junior engineers, or cofacilitate team rituals.

如果你想转向一个更技术化的岗位，就去寻找那些能展现架构思维、或参与系统设计的机会。如果你对工程管理这样的人员领导力路径更感兴趣，就去寻找协调类的角色、辅导更初级的工程师，或是一起主持团队的例会仪式。

And if you're intrigued by the TPM path, use your tech lead day-to-day responsibilities as a springboard, and maybe work more closely with your project manager. Take on more ownership in planning work, offer to manage timelines or dependencies across teams, and step into conversations that require navigating ambiguity.

而如果你对 TPM 这条路心动，就把技术负责人的日常职责当作一块跳板，或许还可以与你的项目经理更紧密地合作。在规划工作中承担更多主人翁责任，主动提出去管理跨团队的时间线或依赖关系，并走进那些需要在模糊中摸索前行的谈话。

Look around your current responsibilities. Chances are, there are already ways to explore these shifts within your existing role.

环顾一下你眼下的职责。很有可能，在你现有的岗位之内，就已经存在着探索这些转变的空间。

These are all ways to stretch into the new role before formally stepping into it.

这些，都是在正式踏入新岗位之前，先让自己“预演式地伸展进去”的方式。

Expand your horizon拓宽你的视野

Get outside of your current environment and company. Learn what other companies are doing, and explore different definitions and formats of the roles you're interested in. Keep in mind that there are opportunities to grow beyond your current company. I know tech leads who were told they'd have to wait years for a transition internally but moved into new roles almost immediately elsewhere. And as I've kept repeating throughout this book, roles mean different things in different companies, so find the environment that defines the role in a way that matches what you actually want to do.

走出你眼下的环境和公司。去了解其他公司在做什么，去探索你所感兴趣岗位的不同定义与形态。请记住：在你现在的公司之外，同样存在着成长的机会。我认识一些技术负责人，他们被告知内部转型得等上好几年，却在别家公司几乎立刻就转入了新岗位。而且正如我在整本书里反复强调的：同一个头衔，在不同公司意味着不同的东西。所以，去找到那样一个环境——它对这个岗位的定义，恰好与你真正想做的事情相匹配。

Give yourself a confidence boost给自己打气、建立信心

Shifting toward a new role can trigger uncertainty, especially when you're stepping into something less familiar. It's normal to doubt yourself or feel like you don't measure up yet. Confidence, though, isn't something you either have or don't; it's something you can actively build.

向新岗位转变，会触发不确定性——尤其是当你正在走进一个不那么熟悉的领域时。怀疑自己、或觉得自己还不够格，都是正常的。然而，信心并不是那种“要么有、要么没有”的东西；它是一种你可以主动去建立的东西。

When I work with tech leads in transition, I often recommend building small, repeatable habits that reinforce your strengths. That could be reviewing positive feedback you've received, keeping a running "done list" to remind yourself of what you've already achieved, or writing down recent wins—even small ones—at the end of the week. Some people record voice notes to talk themselves through tough days; others visualize how they'd show up in the new role and use that to shape their actions now. The key

当我与正在转型中的技术负责人共事时，我常常建议他们去建立一些小而可重复的习惯，来强化自己的优势。这可以是回顾你收到过的正面反馈、持续维护一份“已完成清单”来提醒自己已经取得的成就，或是在每周末写下近期的小胜利——哪怕是很小的。有些人会录下语音备忘，在艰难的日子里自我疏导；另一些人则会在脑海中预演自己在新岗位上的样子，并用这份预演来塑造自己当下的行动。关键

— PDF p.371 —

is not to wait for confidence to appear but to practice the behaviors that build it.

不在于等待信心自己冒出来，而在于去练习那些“能把信心练出来”的行为。

If you want more concrete strategies to try, I've written a guide that collects several of these.

如果你想要更多可以一试的具体策略，我写过一本指南，里面收集了好几种这样的方法。

This transition is an evolving process. Keep checking in with yourself, stay flexible, and remember that career paths are built step-by-step.

这场转型是一个不断演进的过程。持续地关照自己、保持灵活，并记住：职业路径是一步一步走出来的。

Remember: You're Not Locked In记住：你并非被锁死在一条路上

People are often afraid of making the wrong move. But when you don't know exactly what's right for you, any choice that moves you forward is the right one.

人们常常害怕走错一步。但当你并不确切知道什么才适合自己时，任何能让你向前走一步的选择，都是对的选择。

For example, some tech leads decide to go back to being senior developers after trying the role. They often ask me: "Is this a step back in my career?" My answer is always the same: there are no steps back from here. Careers aren't linear; they're made up of experiences that help you learn what fits and what doesn't. Even trying something and realizing it's not for you is a step forward in understanding what you truly want.

举例来说，有些技术负责人在尝试过这个岗位之后，决定回去做高级开发。他们常常问我：“这在我的职业生涯里算不算倒退一步？”我的回答永远是同一个：从这里出发，不存在所谓的“退步”。职业生涯不是一条直线；它是由一段段经历组成的，而这些经历帮你弄清楚什么适合你、什么不适合你。哪怕你尝试了某件事、然后发现它并不适合自己，那也是在“理解自己真正想要什么”这条路上向前迈了一步。

It's OK if your next step doesn't go exactly as planned. What matters is that you keep learning, stay honest with yourself, and remain open to new possibilities. No single role defines your career. Each one is just a chapter in a much longer story.

即使你的下一步没有完全按计划走，也没关系。重要的是你持续学习、对自己保持诚实，并对新的可能性保持开放。没有哪一个岗位能定义你的整个职业生涯。每一个岗位，都只是一个长得多的故事里的一个章节。

And remember, no decision is forever. We are lucky that in the tech industry, we can more easily move back and forth between roles. There's room to explore, adapt, and reframe our path based on evolving interests and needs. I know tech leads who returned to full-time development because they preferred it. I also know others who moved into EM, TPM, or even product roles with ease.

还有，请记住：没有哪个决定是终身不变的。我们很幸运，身处科技行业，可以相对轻松地在不同岗位之间来回切换。我们有空间去探索、去适应、并随着兴趣与需求的演变，重新框定自己的路径。我认识一些技术负责人，因为更喜欢而回到了全职开发；我也认识另一些人，轻松地转入了 EM、TPM、甚至产品岗位。

The most powerful thing you can do for your career is keep moving forward with intention, curiosity, and self-awareness.

你能为自己的职业生涯做的最有力量的一件事，就是带着有意识、好奇心和自我觉察，持续向前。

Key Takeaway本章要点

If there's one thing to take away from this chapter, it's that there is no single "right" next step after being a tech lead, only the one that's right for you.

如果说这一章有什么是你该带走的，那就是：技术负责人之后，并没有一条唯一“正确”的下一步，只有那条“对你来说正确”的下一步。

Whether you choose to stay in the middle—continuing to grow in the tech lead role—lean further into people leadership, deepen your technical influence, or explore something entirely different, the reflections you've done in this chapter are your best guide forward.

无论你选择停留在中间地带——继续在技术负责人岗位上成长——还是进一步走向人员领导力、加深你的技术影响力，又或者去探索全然不同的东西，你在本章中所做的这些反思，都是你向前走时最好的向导。

The real win is choosing with intention: based on what energizes you, where you want to grow, and the kind of impact you want to make.

真正的胜利，在于有意识地做出选择：依据什么让你充满能量、你想在哪里成长，以及你想产生怎样的影响。

— PDF p.372 —

Careers are long. Paths are flexible. And you're allowed to evolve. So wherever you head next, stay curious, stay grounded in what matters to you, and trust that every step forward is part of building a career that truly fits.

职业生涯很长，路径很灵活，而你被允许去不断演化。所以，无论你下一步去向何方，保持好奇、扎根于对你真正重要的东西，并相信：向前的每一步，都是在构建一份真正适合你的职业生涯。

Wrap-Up结语

If you've made it this far, thank you. Writing this book was my way of distilling years of questions, hard lessons, and cherished victories, and my hope is that it helped you feel a little less lost in your tech leadership journey.

如果你一路读到了这里，谢谢你。写这本书，是我把多年来的疑问、惨痛教训和珍视的胜利一一沉淀下来的方式；我希望它能让你在技术领导力的旅程中，少一些迷茫。

We've covered a lot, from the messy middle of transitioning into the tech lead role, to managing people, projects, and stakeholders, to figuring out what comes next. But if there's one message I want to leave you with, it's this:

我们聊了很多——从“转型成为技术负责人”那段乱糟糟的中间地带，到管理人员、项目和干系人，再到琢磨清楚接下来该往哪走。但如果有一句话我想留给你，那就是：

Leadership isn't a destination. It's a series of decisions.

领导力不是一个终点，而是一连串的决定。

Decisions about how you show up for your team. How you grow. Where you invest your energy. And eventually, what you want your career to look like beyond the role you're in today.

这些决定关乎：你如何为你的团队现身、你如何成长、你把精力投向何处，以及最终——你希望自己的职业生涯在今天这个岗位之外，长成什么样子。

Your path won't look like anyone else's. And it shouldn't.

你的路径不会和任何人一样。而它本就不该一样。

There is beauty in ambiguity and complexity. When the role isn't clearly defined, it means you have a chance to shape it, to make it your own. That freedom can feel daunting, but it also means you get to build something that fits you and serves your team in the best way possible.

在模糊与复杂之中，自有其美。当一个岗位没有被清晰定义时，这意味着你有机会去塑造它、把它变成属于你自己的样子。那份自由可能让人望而生畏，但它也意味着：你得以亲手去构建那样一样东西——它既适合你，又能以最好的方式服务你的团队。

This may be the end of this book, but it's not the end of your journey. In fact, it might just be the beginning.

这或许是本书的结尾，但它不是你旅程的终点。事实上，它可能仅仅是个开始。

I continue learning every day about this role, through experience, conversations, and every tech lead I meet. I'll keep sharing what I learn through my newsletter. Follow along if you'd like more templates, tools, stories, and reflections on these topics.

关于这个岗位，我每天都还在学习——通过亲身经历、通过对话，也通过我遇到的每一位技术负责人。我会继续通过我的通讯分享所学。如果你想获得更多关于这些主题的模板、工具、故事和反思，欢迎跟着一起看。

And if you ever have a question, want to share your perspective, or just want to connect, don't hesitate to reach out. I'm always open to new ways of thinking—and who knows, maybe you'll even change my mind about something. ;)

而如果你有任何问题、想分享你的看法，或是只是想认识一下，都别犹豫，尽管联系我。我永远对新的思考方式保持开放——谁知道呢，说不定你还会在某件事上改变我的想法呢。;)

Good luck!

祝你好运！
